title: NGC 7252: Spiral Disk and Globular Star Clusters at the Core of a Colliding Galaxy
caption: The core of the colliding galaxy NGC 7252, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: : B. Whitmore (STScI), and NASA Co-investigators: : Francois Schweizer of the Carnegie Institution of Washington, Washington, D.C., and Claus Leitherer, Kirk Borne, and Carmelle Robert of STScI.

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A small pinwheel of gas and stars glows at the core of the peculiar galaxy NGC 7252, surrounded by about 40 very bright, young globular star clusters. The spiral looks uncannily like a whole galaxy seen face-on, yet it is only 10,000 light-years across, roughly a twentieth of the galaxy's full width. NGC 7252 lies some 300 million light-years away in the constellation Aquarius.

The clusters gather near the core. They are about 60 light-years across, the same size as the globular clusters orbiting the Milky Way, but most are estimated to be only 50 to 500 million years old. They appear to have formed after two disc-shaped galaxies collided about a billion years ago, and the collision probably fed the central disc as well.

That makes NGC 7252 strong evidence for a long-debated idea, that giant elliptical galaxies form when disc galaxies merge. Its young clusters are considered forerunners of the Milky Way's ancient ones.
scale: The whole picture spans 46,000 light-years, according to NASA.

understand.summary: A visible-light image from Hubble's original Wide Field and Planetary Camera in its PC mode, sharpened by computer image reconstruction. It is shown in false color, and the color mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The colors are false and the picture was computer-processed, so it does not show what an eye would see.

explore: Hubble's sharpness let astronomers measure the clusters' sizes even at this distance. Each spans about 0.04 arc seconds, roughly how big a dime looks from 60 miles away. Some outshine the Milky Way's globulars by up to a few hundred times, thanks to many hot, short-lived blue stars. The galaxy's long tails are clear signs of a merger.
sources: NASA release: What Happens When Galaxies Collide? Hubble Space Telescope Finds New Surprises
